498.title: Re'eh: open thy hand (Deuteronomy 15:7–8)
498.hook: don't harden your heart or shut your hand; "thou shalt surely open thy hand"
498.howItsDone: Many Jewish homes keep a tzedakah box, called a pushke, and drop coins in before the Sabbath; Jewish law sets a tenth of income as a common measure and Maimonides' eight levels are widely taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday, re'eh: see the fork in the road, this day. Your line was see the choice. Did you catch yours? Today, a choice that comes up every time someone asks you for help. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

A man is standing at the light with a cardboard sign. You see him from three cars back. And in the seconds before you reach him, a whole conversation happens inside you. Do I have cash? Will he spend it well? Is it safe to roll the window down? The light's about to change anyway. Often, by the time you've finished thinking, the moment's gone. The Torah describes that inner conversation surprisingly well, and it names the two body parts where it happens: the heart, and the hand.
screen: `A SIGN AT THE LIGHT.` → `THE CONVERSATION INSIDE YOU.` → `THE HEART, AND THE HAND.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "thou shalt not harden thy heart, nor shut thy hand from thy needy brother; but thou shalt surely open thy hand unto him." Notice the order. The heart hardens first, then the hand closes. Giving starts inside, before any money moves. And notice the doubling. Surely open thy hand is, in Hebrew, patoach tiftach: open, you shall open. The rabbis read the double verb as open, and open again. Not once. The verse goes on: lend him sufficient for his need. His need, not your idea of his need. The word for all of this in Jewish life is today's word, tzedakah. It's often translated charity, but the root is tzedek, justice, righteousness. Charity sounds like something extra you choose to do when you feel generous. Tzedakah is closer to what's right, what's owed, part of how a just society works. And it reaches the giver too. The great medieval teacher Maimonides laid out eight levels of tzedakah. Giving grudgingly is the lowest. Giving before you're asked is higher. Giving so neither side knows the other is higher still. And the highest of all: helping someone with a loan, a partnership or a job, so they won't need to ask again. A few verses later the Torah says plainly that there will always be poor people in the land. That's not a shrug. It's the reason the hand must keep opening.
screen: `THE HEART HARDENS, THE HAND CLOSES.` · `PATOACH TIFTACH: OPEN, AND OPEN.` · `TZEDAKAH, FROM TZEDEK: JUSTICE.` · `EIGHT LEVELS, A JOB AT THE TOP.` · then, large: `OPEN THY HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give without hesitating. Settle, and breathe. Make two fists, and notice how they feel. Tight, ready, closed. Now slowly open them, palms up, resting on your knees. Stay like that. Think of the last time someone asked you for help and you felt your heart start to harden. What was the conversation inside you? You don't have to judge it. Just notice it, palms open. Then decide on one gift you'll give today, quickly, before the conversation starts. The bell holds the time.
Tzedakah. Giving to those in need, from tzedek, justice. Not an extra, but part of what's right.
Your line: open thy hand. Today, when someone asks, give before your heart has time to harden. Small is fine. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

its root is tzedek, justice: closer to what's right and owed.
the verse says the heart hardens before the hand shuts

Maimonides ranks giving a job above giving a gift
the highest level helps someone so they won't need to ask again.

options: give a large gift with your name on it.
help someone with a loan, a partnership or a job.

fork.reveal: the top level strengthens someone so they won't need to ask again.

what it means: giving as justice, with an open heart first, sized to the other person's real need.
what a scholar hears: patoach tiftach, the doubled verb; Maimonides' eight levels in the Laws of Gifts to the Poor, chapter ten.

499.title: Re'eh: the release (Deuteronomy 15:1–2)
499.hook: every seventh year debts are released
499.howItsDone: In the land of Israel, observant Jewish farmers still keep the shmita year for the land, and many observant Jews sign a prozbul before the end of the seventh year so that loans aren't canceled.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzedakah: the heart and the hand, open and open again. Your line was open thy hand. What did you give before you could talk yourself out of it? Today, a law that wipes the slate clean. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

Picture the moment a student loan is finally paid off, or a medical bill forgiven, or a credit card cleared. People describe it physically. I could breathe again. A weight off my chest. Now imagine a society where that moment was built into the calendar. Every seven years, for everyone, at once. Not because a bank decided to be kind, but because the law said so. That's the seventh year in Deuteronomy. And the Mishnah remembers what happened when people actually tried to live by it.
screen: `PAID OFF: I COULD BREATHE.` → `BUILT INTO THE CALENDAR.` → `WHAT HAPPENED WHEN THEY TRIED.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release." The Hebrew word is shmita, a letting drop. Exodus already used that verb for the land: in the seventh year, let it drop, let it lie fallow. Deuteronomy uses it for debts. Each creditor lets go of what he lent to his neighbor, and doesn't press for it. The point is plain. Debt piles up. Without a reset, the poor get poorer and people get trapped. The release lets a whole society start over. But the Torah knows people. A few verses later it warns: don't let a base thought into your heart, saying the seventh year is close, and refuse to lend. Because of course that's exactly what happens. If every loan will be wiped out in a year, why lend? By the time of Hillel, around the turn of the common era, that's what people were doing. The Mishnah says he saw that people had stopped lending to one another, and the poor were the ones getting hurt. So Hillel created a legal document called the prozbul. A lender could hand his debts over to the court, and debts held by a court weren't released. Lending started again. Some later teachers were uneasy, and the debate about Hillel's fix runs through the Talmud. But the motive is clear: a law meant to protect the poor had started to hurt them, and Hillel acted to protect them again.
screen: `SHMITA: A LETTING DROP.` · `A RESET FOR A WHOLE SOCIETY.` · `PEOPLE STOPPED LENDING.` · `HILLEL'S PROZBUL.` · then, large: `RELEASE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: release someone from something owed. Settle, and breathe. Think about what other people owe you. Maybe money. More often, it's something else: an apology, a favor returned, a call back, credit for something you did. Let one of those debts come to mind. Notice the weight of holding it. Then ask: what would it be like to let this one drop? Not because they've earned it. Because the year has turned. If you can, let it go, here, now. The bell holds the time.
Re'eh. See. The portion that sets out the seventh-year release of debts, a whole society letting go at once.
Your line: release. Today, let one small debt drop, of money, time or an apology, and tell no one. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

500.title: Re'eh: rejoice together (Deuteronomy 16:11, 14)
500.hook: rejoice at the festival with the servant, the stranger, the orphan and the widow
500.howItsDone: Jews treat joy on the festivals, especially Sukkot, as a commandment, and many families make a point of inviting guests, newcomers and people who would otherwise be alone to holiday meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shmita, the seventh-year release, and Hillel's fix. Your line was release. What did you let drop? Today is day five hundred, and fittingly, the Torah commands a party. Day five hundred.

Think of a wedding you went to, a really good one. The music, the dancing, the food. Now think about who was there. Family, old friends, coworkers. Who wasn't? The neighbor who lives alone. The new guy at work who doesn't know anyone yet. Nobody left them out on purpose. They just weren't on the list. Most celebrations are drawn in a circle around the people we already love. The Torah's festival law draws that circle, and then keeps going, naming people one by one until the guest list looks very different.
screen: `A REALLY GOOD WEDDING.` → `WHO WASN'T THERE?` → `THE CIRCLE KEEPS GOING.`

segments.voice: Deuteronomy sixteen walks through the three pilgrimage festivals: Passover, Shavuot, and Sukkot. For Shavuot and Sukkot, it commands joy. In the old Jewish translation, of Sukkot: "And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast." The Hebrew word for that joy is today's word, simcha. And then the guest list. Thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, and thy servants, and the Levite, who has no land of his own, and the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your gates. Rashi, the great medieval commentator, counts them in two groups of four. Four are yours: son, daughter, manservant, maidservant. Four are God's: the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, the widow. And he imagines God saying: if you make Mine happy, I'll make yours happy. Maimonides makes it sharper. In his law code he writes that someone who locks the gates of his courtyard and eats and drinks with his family, but doesn't feed the poor and the grieving, isn't having the joy of a commandment at all. He's having the joy of his stomach. So in Jewish law, simcha isn't only a feeling you have. It's something you make, and you can't fully make it alone or only with your own. Joy, in this chapter, is measured partly by who else is at the table.
screen: `THREE FESTIVALS, AND A COMMAND TO REJOICE.` · `FOUR OF YOURS, FOUR OF MINE.` · `THE JOY OF HIS STOMACH.` · `WHO ELSE IS AT THE TABLE?` · then, large: `REJOICE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: include someone in a celebration. Settle, and breathe. You've reached five hundred days of this. That's worth a small celebration, and it's yours. Now think about the next gathering in your life: a birthday, a holiday meal, a Sabbath dinner, a game night, even coffee. Picture the table. Now picture Rashi's other four. Who in your life is the stranger, the one alone, the one grieving, the one without people nearby? Choose one to invite. The bell holds the time.
Simcha. Joy, the festival kind, commanded in Deuteronomy and made bigger by who you bring in.
Your line: rejoice together. Today, invite one person who wouldn't be on the usual list. Day five hundred.

501.title: Re'eh: as you were blessed (Deuteronomy 16:17)
501.hook: each gives according to the blessing they have received
501.howItsDone: The reading that ends with this verse is used on the last days of the pilgrimage festivals, and in many synagogues, when Yizkor is recited on those days, people pledge charity in memory of relatives who have died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, simcha: four of yours and four of God's at the festival table. Your line was rejoice together. Who did you invite? Today, the last verse of Re'eh, about what each guest brings. Day five hundred one.

Every office has done it. Someone's leaving, and an envelope goes around for a gift. Somebody suggests everyone put in twenty dollars. And immediately it's awkward. For the manager, twenty is nothing. For the part-time assistant saving for rent, it's a real bite. A flat amount sounds fair, and isn't. A percentage sounds cold, and is fairer. Nobody quite knows how to say it out loud. The last verse of Re'eh says it out loud, in a handful of words, about pilgrims arriving at the Temple three times a year.
screen: `THE ENVELOPE GOES AROUND.` → `TWENTY DOLLARS, FAIR OR NOT?` → `THE VERSE SAYS IT OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Three times a year, the chapter says, at Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, the people go up to the place God chooses. And, in the old Jewish translation: "they shall not appear before the LORD empty." Everyone brings something. But how much? The next verse answers: "Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD thy God which He hath given thee." In Hebrew, ish k'matnat yado: each person according to the gift of his hand. No flat fee. No single price. The measure is what you've been given. The Mishnah, in tractate Chagigah, works it out for the festival offerings. Someone with many mouths to feed and little money brings what they can, shaped to their household. Someone with much brings more. Same command, different amounts. Notice the two sides of it. Nobody comes empty. Even the poorest pilgrim brings something, and so stands in the courtyard as a giver, not just a receiver. And nobody hides behind a small number when they've been given a great deal. The verse doesn't shame anyone in either direction. It asks one quiet question: what have you been blessed with? This verse also ends a Torah reading used on the last days of the festivals, and in many synagogues those are days when the memorial prayer, Yizkor, is said, and people pledge gifts in memory of those they've lost. Giving, again, according to what you were given, including the people who gave it.
screen: `NOT EMPTY.` · `K'MATNAT YADO: THE GIFT OF HIS HAND.` · `MANY MOUTHS, LITTLE MONEY.` · `A GIVER, NOT JUST A RECEIVER.` · then, large: `ACCORDING TO YOUR BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give in proportion to what you have. Settle, and breathe. Take honest stock, not just of money. Time. Health. A skill. Free evenings. A car. A calm temperament. Patience with kids. Which of these do you have more of this season than the people around you? Now think of one place to give from that surplus, in proportion. If you have little money but a lot of time, the gift might be time. If you have little time but more money, maybe the reverse. The bell holds the time.
Re'eh. See. The portion that ends with each pilgrim giving according to the blessing they've been given.
Your line: according to your blessing. Today, give one thing you have more of than you need, sized to what you've been given. Day five hundred one.

502.title: Shoftim: judges at the gates (Deuteronomy 16:18)
502.hook: judges in every town; Hasidic teachers read the gates as eyes, ears and mouth
502.howItsDone: Shoftim is usually read in synagogues around the start of Elul, the month before Rosh Hashanah, and Hasidic and other teachers often use its opening verse to speak about guarding the eyes, ears and mouth as part of the season's self-examination.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pilgrims who gave according to the gift of their hand. Your line was according to your blessing. What did you give from your surplus? Today a new portion, Shoftim, starts at the town gate. Day five hundred two.

In an ancient town, the gate wasn't just a door in the wall. It was the town square, the courthouse and the marketplace at once. Elders sat there. Deals were witnessed there. In the book of Ruth, Boaz goes up to the gate, sits down, and settles a family matter in front of ten elders. Everything that came into the town, people, goods, news, trouble, came through the gate, and whoever sat there decided what to do about it. That's where the new portion begins.
screen: `THE GATE: SQUARE, COURT, MARKET.` → `BOAZ SITS AT THE GATE.` → `EVERYTHING COMES THROUGH.`

segments.voice: The first verse, in the old Jewish translation: "Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates." Shoftim means judges, and it names the portion. The plain sense is civic. Every town needs courts, and people to enforce what courts decide, right where life passes through. Justice shouldn't be a long trip to a distant capital. It should sit at your own gate. But notice the odd little word thee. Shalt thou make thee. In Hebrew, lecha: for yourself. Judges for yourself? Later teachers seized on that. Hasidic masters, building on earlier mystics, read the verse inward. A person is a town too, they said, with gates of their own. The eyes, the ears, the mouth, and some add the nostrils. Everything that enters you comes through those gates: what you look at, what you listen to, what you take in. And everything that leaves you goes out through one of them: what you say. So set judges at your gates. Not to shut them. A town with its gates welded shut starves. But to notice what's coming in and going out, and to decide. And there's a calendar reason this reading lands well. Shoftim is usually read in the month of Elul, the weeks before Rosh Hashanah, when many Jews take stock of themselves. A portion about courts at the gates arrives just as people start judging their own year.
screen: `SHOFTIM: JUDGES.` · `JUSTICE AT YOUR OWN GATE.` · `LECHA: FOR YOURSELF.` · `EYES, EARS, MOUTH.` · then, large: `GUARD YOUR GATES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: guard one of your own gates. Settle, and breathe. Close your eyes, and notice them resting. Notice your ears, what's coming in right now. Notice your mouth, closed. Now think about the last day. What came in through your eyes that you'd rather not have let in? What through your ears? What went out of your mouth that you'd take back? Pick one gate. Not all of them. Decide one small thing that gate's judge will watch for today. The bell holds the time.
Shoftim. Judges. The name of the portion, from its first command: judges and officers in all your gates.
Your line: guard your gates. Today, stand at the gate you chose, and let one thing not come in, or not go out. Day five hundred two.

503.title: Shoftim: justice, justice (Deuteronomy 16:20)
503.hook: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow"; the doubled word means just ends by just means
503.howItsDone: Tzedek tzedek tirdof is one of the most quoted verses in Jewish life, inscribed in synagogues and courthouses and cited by Jewish movements for social and legal justice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, judges at the gates: the town's and your own. Your line was guard your gates. Which gate did you stand at? Today, two verses later, one of the most quoted lines in the Torah. Day five hundred three.

You've probably seen it on a poster, a courthouse wall, or a protest sign. Two words, repeated. Justice, justice. In a language where a single word is usually enough, the Torah says this one twice, and anyone who has read the verse closely has asked why. Teachers have been answering for two thousand years. The answers don't cancel each other out. They stack, like layers. Each one turns the doubled word a little, and catches a different light.
screen: `ON A POSTER, A WALL, A SIGN.` → `ONE WORD, SAID TWICE.` → `THE ANSWERS STACK.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow, that thou mayest live, and inherit the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee." In Hebrew, tzedek tzedek tirdof. Tzedek is today's word: justice, rightness. It's the root of tzedakah, which we met a few days ago. And tirdof doesn't really mean follow. It means pursue, chase, run after. Justice isn't something you wait for. You go after it. Now the double. The Talmud, in Sanhedrin, offers a few readings. One: the first justice is strict law, the second is compromise. A court should know when to rule, and when to help two sides settle. Another: pursue a good court, travel to the wisest judges. And then a reading that's become famous much later, often attributed to the Hasidic teacher Rabbi Simcha Bunim of Peshischa: pursue justice justly. Just ends by just means. You can't chase justice by cheating, by lying, by trampling people on the way. The way you pursue it has to be as just as the place you're trying to reach. And the verse right before gives a sharp example: a judge must not take a gift, because a gift blinds the eyes of the wise. A bribe doesn't just tempt; it changes what you can see. So the doubled word guards both ends. The goal must be just. And the road there must be just too.
screen: `TZEDEK TZEDEK TIRDOF.` · `NOT FOLLOW: PURSUE.` · `STRICT LAW, AND COMPROMISE.` · `JUST ENDS BY JUST MEANS.` · then, large: `JUSTICE, JUSTICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be fair in how you're fair. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're in the right about. A dispute with a sibling, a cause you care about, an argument at work. You may well be right. Now look only at the means. How have you been pursuing it? With accurate words, or exaggerations? With respect for the other side, or contempt? With patience, or pressure? Find one place where the road has been less just than the goal. Decide how you'll walk it differently. The bell holds the time.
Tzedek. Justice, rightness. Said twice in Shoftim, and pursued, not waited for.
Your line: justice, justice. Today, in one thing you're right about, make sure the way you argue it is fair too. Day five hundred three.

504.title: Shoftim: even the king reads (Deuteronomy 17:18–20)
504.hook: the king writes his own copy of the Torah so his heart isn't lifted up
504.tomorrow: Shoftim: is the tree a man? (Deuteronomy 20:19)
504.howItsDone: Jewish law counts writing a Torah scroll as a commandment for every Jew; many fulfill it today by sponsoring or writing a single letter in a community's new scroll, and the king's special scroll is discussed in the Talmud and Maimonides.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzedek tzedek tirdof: pursue justice, and pursue it justly. Your line was justice, justice. Was the way you argued fair? Today, the law for the most powerful person in the land. Day five hundred four.

In the ancient world, a king was the law. His word settled things. His image was on the coins. Scribes wrote down his victories and carved them into stone. The idea that a king might have to sit down with a pen and copy out somebody else's law, by hand, every word, and then read it every day of his life, would have sounded absurd in most royal courts. Deuteronomy's chapter on kings is short, and it's mostly a list of limits. And it ends with homework.
screen: `THE KING WAS THE LAW.` → `COPY SOMEONE ELSE'S LAW?` → `A CHAPTER OF LIMITS.`

segments.voice: First the limits. If Israel sets a king over itself, he must not pile up horses, or take many wives, or heap up silver and gold. Power, pleasure, money: the three things kings usually collect. Then the homework. In the old Jewish translation: when he sits on his throne, "he shall write him a copy of this law in a book." And it shall be with him, "and he shall read therein all the days of his life." Why? The verse says it plainly: "that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren." Brothers. The king is still one of them. The Talmud, in Sanhedrin, adds that the king actually writes a scroll of his own, kept with him wherever he goes, even into battle. And it notes that every Jew is commanded to write a Torah scroll; the king just has an extra one. The phrase for a copy of this law is mishneh hatorah. It's where Deuteronomy gets its Greek name, second law. And over a thousand years later, Maimonides borrowed the same words for his great law code, the Mishneh Torah. The king reading every day is a picture of power under something bigger than itself. Not the king's word over the law, but the law over the king's word. Reading isn't a reward for the powerful. It's a brake.
